findings.title: Dummy-hash timing cover inverts the side channel: misses cost ~2x a real verify
findings.evidence: Line 40 routes misses to dummyHash(); dummyHash (lines 7-15) uses a function-level 'static $hash = null' that is re-initialised on every PHP request, so lines 9-12 run a full 'password_hash(bin2hex(random_bytes(16)), PASSWORD_DEFAULT)' during the login request, and line 41 then runs 'password_verify' on it. A non-existent account therefore does hash+verify while an existing account with a wrong password does only verify.
findings.recommendation: Make the dummy hash a precomputed constant (e.g. a checked-in known bcrypt string literal, or generated once at bootstrap/cache warmup, never inside the request), so the miss path performs exactly one password_verify with the same algorithm and cost as stored hashes. Also pin the algorithm and cost explicitly instead of PASSWORD_DEFAULT so the dummy verify cost cannot drift from the stored-hash cost.

findings.title: Only a minimum length is enforced; bcrypt silently truncates at 72 bytes
findings.evidence: Line 19 validates with 'if (strlen($password) < 12) {' only, and line 24 hashes with 'password_hash($password, PASSWORD_DEFAULT)'. With the supported default (bcrypt) any password longer than 72 bytes is truncated, so two distinct long passwords sharing a 72-byte prefix both verify against the same hash; strlen is also byte-based, so a 12-byte minimum can be fewer than 12 characters for multi-byte input.
findings.recommendation: Enforce an explicit upper bound (reject passwords > 72 bytes for bcrypt, or pre-hash with SHA-384/base64 before bcrypt, or use PASSWORD_ARGON2ID), and use mb_strlen for the minimum-length policy. Apply the same policy on both register and login-compare paths.

findings.title: Rehash UPDATE has no old-hash predicate, so it can revert a concurrent password change
findings.evidence: The statement at line 48 is 'UPDATE users SET password_hash = :hash WHERE id = :id' and executes with line 50 '['hash' => $newHash, 'id' => $user['id']]'. If the user's password is changed by another session between the SELECT on line 38 and this UPDATE, the rehash writes a hash derived from the stale plaintext and silently rolls the account back to the old password.
findings.recommendation: Make the write conditional on the hash still being the one that was verified (WHERE id = :id AND password_hash = :old_hash) and check rowCount(); treat a 0-row update as a benign no-op rather than overwriting.

findings.title: Unhandled exception in best-effort rehash turns a valid login into a 500
findings.evidence: Line 50 executes the rehash UPDATE without any try/catch. With the normal ERRMODE_EXCEPTION settings a lock-wait timeout, deadlock, or a row deleted concurrently makes the whole attemptLogin throw after the password has already been verified, so a correct login fails; under ERRMODE_SILENT, prepare() at line 47 can return false and line 50 fatals on a bool.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the rehash in try/catch: log the failure and continue returning the authenticated user, since rehashing is best-effort. Optionally assert the prepare() result is a PDOStatement before use.
